title: Benchmarks with RTX 3080
summary: What I wanted from a 10 GB RTX 3080, the tests I wrote to find out, and how I tuned engines and models until it fit. Test code and cases are published.

posts.title: The chip, and what I want from it
posts.summary: What an RTX 3080 is on paper, the job I bought it for, and the questions this series answers with measurements.
posts.verdict: A 10 GB, 760 GB/s card should fit a quantized 8B model and generate fast on paper. Sharing the card and decision quality are the open risks.

posts.title: The tests I wrote
posts.summary: Four instruments, 82 decision cases and 15 tool-calling prompts, all published. What each one measures and how I kept it honest.
posts.verdict: Speed and fit can be repeated by anyone from the published folder. Quality rests on one suite I wrote for my own agent.

posts.title: vLLM first, and why it did not stay
posts.summary: April to September. The serious serving engine took the whole card, sharing the card did not hold, and the budget explains both.
posts.verdict: vLLM claimed 8.5 of 10 GiB for a 7B model and sharing failed twice, so Ollama became the single GPU tenant.

posts.title: Fitting a real model in 10 GB
posts.summary: September to October. A 14B, a 9B and an 8B on the same card, and the arithmetic that predicts which fits before you download anything.
posts.verdict: Qwen3 8B at 40k context with a q8_0 KV cache: the only candidate that is fully resident and best at choosing tools.

posts.title: Raw speed against the ceilings
posts.summary: November 11. The datasheet drew two ceilings. A sweep measured an 8B model and a 35B mixture-of-experts model against them, and one prediction was wrong.
posts.verdict: The 8B generates at 79% of the bandwidth ceiling and reads prompts faster than my ceiling allowed, so the ceiling was wrong. The 35B runs but is 1.8x slower to generate.

posts.title: Engines head to head
posts.summary: Ollama against the llama.cpp server underneath it, then a third engine that cannot reuse a prompt. Decode speed, first-token time and load.
posts.verdict: Stay on Ollama: it costs 2 to 8% decode speed. Strata cannot reuse a prompt, which makes a warm start 42x slower.

posts.title: Does a bigger model pay off?
posts.summary: Speed is settled, so I measured decisions. My agent's suite on Qwen3 8B and a 35B mixture-of-experts model, then the whole series scored against the goal.
posts.verdict: Stay on the 8B: the 35B scores 58.9% against 61.6 to 62.8% and takes over twice as long. Hardware is not the blocker; decision quality is unproven.

title: WTF is Agent?
summary: How an autonomous agent actually works, one component at a time, from my own build. The anatomy, the design decisions, what I deleted, and a survey of what already exists.

posts.title: The anatomy of an agent
posts.summary: What an autonomous agent is made of, as a conceptual system design, the order I built it in, and the six rules I followed.
posts.verdict: An agent is a model in a loop plus seven things around it. The loop, memory and toolbox are the spine; the rest is where I rebuilt the most.

posts.title: Memory: remember, cite, forget
posts.summary: Three layers, one provenance trail, and a forget that follows it. What I built, rebuilt and surveyed for an agent's long-term memory.
posts.verdict: Store the raw text, keep facts small, derive everything else, and make every belief point back to its source so it can be traced and forgotten. The design is built; its evaluation is not.

posts.title: The toolbox: one door to every tool
posts.summary: Hundreds of tools cannot all sit in a prompt. A catalog that holds the logins, shows tools on demand and lets the model write code against it.
posts.verdict: One door that holds every login, a typed catalog the model searches, and code instead of one tool call per turn. The agent never holds a secret.

posts.title: The harness: a loop that survives
posts.summary: The control loop around the model, made durable and interruptible, with almost no opinions of its own. What I kept from an existing agent, what I changed and what I deleted.
posts.verdict: Keep the model's loop, change where it runs: durable, one active turn per conversation, interrupts as signals. Let the model steer and delete the routers, lanes and planners that tried to help.

posts.title: Context and skills: what the model reads
posts.summary: The prompt is a view over everything that was said, not a copy. How I keep it small without losing anything, and how skills turn procedure into scripts.
posts.verdict: Keep everything, show the model a summarised view, store big results as files, and compact in two tiers. Put mechanical steps in skill scripts, because an agent's latency is its number of model steps.

posts.title: Runtime and sandbox: where agent code runs
posts.summary: An agent that writes code needs somewhere to run it that holds no secrets and no network. Three designs in one day, and the engine that won.
posts.verdict: One execution interface with several light engines, inside a sandbox that has no network and no secrets. I built a microVM per session first and replaced it within a day, because a pure function should not need a VM.

posts.title: Waking, asking, stopping
posts.summary: How an agent starts without being asked, pauses to ask a person, and stops before it does damage. Three designs for waking, one primitive for asking.
posts.verdict: An agent only needs a wake when its own reasoning is needed later; everything else is a notification. Asking is a durable pause, approvals are the same pause, and stopping is a clean result, not a crash.

posts.title: Knowing it works: evals
posts.summary: A labelled suite for the one decision everything depends on, run on every model before I build on it. What it caught, and the ceiling I still cannot explain.
posts.verdict: Measure a judgement before building on it: labelled cases, several samples, a held-out set. It already killed one design. My own suite has a ceiling I have not explained, so the scores are capped.

posts.title: What I deleted
posts.summary: Thirteen things I built and then removed, why each went, and the design rules that were left standing. The finale of the build.
posts.verdict: I deleted nearly as much as I kept, and the reasons repeat: the model did it better, it duplicated something, it sat in the wrong layer, or it was heavier than the job. The design is what survived.

posts.title: AI is a label, not a thing
posts.summary: AI" covers a stack of ideas from rule-based programs to language models. Knowing which layer someone means clears up most of the confusion.
posts.verdict: AI is a stack of ideas: AI, machine learning, deep learning, language models. Ask which layer someone means.

posts.title: Machine learning is fitting a curve
posts.summary: Instead of writing rules, you show a program examples and let it find the rules. Training, inference and overfitting in one small example.
posts.verdict: Machine learning finds rules from examples by nudging parameters to shrink the error. Only data the model has never seen counts.

posts.title: Neural networks are lots of tiny dials
posts.summary: A neuron is a weighted sum plus a bend. Stack millions of them and you have a network, and a reason GPUs matter.
posts.verdict: A neural network is stacked weighted sums with a bend, trained by gradient descent. It is matrix multiplication, which is why GPUs matter.

posts.title: Language models are autocomplete at scale
posts.summary: Predict the next token, over and over. How that one trick produces fluent text, why it also produces confident nonsense, and what the knobs do.
posts.verdict: A language model predicts the next token. Its output is fluent and plausible but unverified, so give it sources and check what matters.
